Three rules for giving advice, and the first one will save you the most time. Rule one: ask what they have already decided. Most people have decided, and what they want from you is permission, so the question that actually helps is not what should I do, it is what are you tempted to do. Rule two: never say you have to. Nobody has to do anything, and the phrase makes people defend the option you are arguing against. Rule three, and this is the one that changes conversations. Say what you would do, not what they should do. It is exactly the same advice, it costs the same number of words, and it is far easier to hear, because it leaves the decision where it belongs.

Hi, sorry to call so late. I need a second opinion and you are the only person who will tell me the truth. They want me to sign on Friday. I could sign, or I could ask for two more weeks to look at the numbers properly. My worry is that if I ask for more time they will think I am not serious and go to somebody else, and honestly that may not even be true, it may just be me. So here is what I want from you. Do not tell me what I should do. Tell me what you would do, in my position, on Friday morning. Call me back whenever.

He says he would ask what changes in a year. She asks whether he would not play it safe, and he asks what she is tempted to do.
